title: How to Tell When to Keep Going (and When to Run)
author: Graham, Molly
summary: Molly Graham interviews Claire Hughes Johnson -- former COO of Stripe and author of Scaling People -- on how to distinguish between the inevitable messiness of a healthy startup and the structural dysfunction that signals it's time to leave. All success stories feel chaotic from the inside, which makes it hard to diagnose whether the mess you're experiencing is formative or toxic. Hughes Johnson offers practical diagnostic questions: Are the right problems being wrestled with, even if imperfectly? Is the leadership honest about what's broken? Is there learning embedded in the failure? The article argues that the impulse to flee is normal at certain growth stages, and that seasoned operators develop a pattern-recognition ability to distinguish 'good hard' from 'bad hard.' Both authors emphasize that the ability to tolerate productive ambiguity is itself a learnable leadership competency.
points: All success stories look like chaos from the inside: the mess of a high-growth environment is not itself diagnostic -- what matters is whether the mess is productive or structural.
Claire Hughes Johnson's diagnostic: ask whether leadership is honest about what's broken -- organizations that acknowledge problems and wrestle with them intelligently are worth staying in.
'Good hard' vs. 'bad hard' is a learnable distinction: experienced operators develop the pattern recognition to tell formative friction from toxic dysfunction.
The impulse to leave is often a growth signal, not an exit signal: recognizing this distinction requires the self-awareness to separate discomfort from damage.
Productive ambiguity tolerance is a core leadership competency: the ability to operate effectively without clarity or credit is what separates leaders who can scale from those who cannot.
quotes: All success stories feel like a mess from the inside. Claire Hughes Johnson on how to tell the difference between normal mess and the kind that should send you running.
The question is not 'Is this hard?' The question is 'Is this the right kind of hard?' The best environments are hard in ways that build you. The worst are hard in ways that diminish you.

Leaders who can acknowledge what's broken and work on it honestly -- even while the company is growing -- are worth following. Leaders who pretend nothing is broken are a sign to start watching the exits.
The discomfort of growth and the discomfort of toxicity can feel identical from the inside. Pattern recognition takes time and experience to develop.
Productive ambiguity -- the ability to act effectively without clarity, credit, or complete information -- is the skill that makes scaling possible.
